_about: Plain-English help shown in the emulator's details panel. Keys under 'settings' are setting names as shown in the BIOS; a '#' stands for any number (e.g. 'CPU Core# Voltage' matches Core0 and Core1). Edit freely.

generic_options.Auto: Let the BIOS decide. It picks a safe value based on your CPU, memory and board. This is the right choice unless you have a specific reason to change it.
generic_options.Manual: You set the value yourself. Extra fields appear underneath where you type it.
generic_options.Offset Mode: Keep the automatic value, but add or subtract a fixed amount from it.
generic_options.Override Mode: Ignore the automatic value and use exactly the number you type.
generic_options.Ignore: Hide this reading and don't warn about it.

glossary.BCLK: Base clock: the 100 MHz reference 'heartbeat' that CPU, memory and PCIe speeds are multiplied from. Changing it shifts everything at once.
glossary.FCLK: Infinity Fabric clock: the speed of the internal link between the CPU's core chiplets and its memory controller.
glossary.UCLK: Memory-controller clock. Ideally it matches the memory clock (1:1).
glossary.MCLK: Memory clock: half the DDR5 'MT/s' number (DDR5-5600 runs at 2800 MHz MCLK).
glossary.CCD: Core Complex Die: one of the CPU's core chiplets. A 9975WX has 4 CCDs with 8 cores each.
glossary.CCX: Core Complex: a group of cores sharing a cache. On Zen 5 each CCD is one CCX.
glossary.PBO: Precision Boost Overdrive: lets the CPU boost higher and longer by raising AMD's power and current limits.
glossary.Precision Boost Overdrive: Lets the CPU boost higher and longer by raising AMD's power and current limits.
glossary.PPT: Package Power Tracking: the total power (watts) the CPU socket is allowed to draw.
glossary.TDC: Thermal Design Current: the sustained current (amps) the voltage regulators may supply.
glossary.EDC: Electrical Design Current: the short-burst peak current (amps) the voltage regulators may supply.
glossary.SMT: Simultaneous Multi-Threading: runs 2 threads per core (AMD's version of Hyper-Threading). Off = 32 threads instead of 64 on a 9975WX.
glossary.EXPO: AMD EXtended Profiles for Overclocking: speed/timing/voltage presets stored on the memory sticks by the manufacturer.
glossary.DOCP: ASUS's way of loading Intel XMP memory profiles on AMD boards.
glossary.XMP: Intel eXtreme Memory Profile: memory speed presets stored on the sticks.
glossary.JEDEC: The industry-standard memory speed every stick supports without overclocking (4800 MT/s for your DIMMs).
glossary.SPD: A tiny chip on each memory stick that stores its speeds, timings and profiles.
glossary.PMIC: Power-management chip on each DDR5 stick that makes the memory's own voltages.
glossary.VDD: Main supply voltage (for memory: the DRAM chips themselves).
glossary.VPP: Memory 'activation' voltage used when opening rows (normally 1.8 V).
glossary.VSOC: SoC voltage: powers the CPU's I/O die (memory controller, Infinity Fabric, PCIe).
glossary.VDDSOC: SoC voltage: powers the CPU's I/O die (memory controller, Infinity Fabric, PCIe).
glossary.VDDIO: Memory-interface voltage on the CPU side.
glossary.VDDP: Voltage for the memory PHY (the CPU circuitry that talks to the DIMMs).
glossary.VDDG: Voltage for the Infinity Fabric links between chiplets.
glossary.VID: Voltage ID: the voltage the CPU asks the regulators for.
glossary.VRM: Voltage Regulator Module: the power stages around the socket that feed the CPU.
glossary.LLC: Load-line calibration: how much the CPU voltage is allowed to droop under heavy load.
glossary.Load-line Calibration: Controls how much CPU voltage droops under heavy load. Higher levels = less droop (steadier voltage, more heat).
glossary.Curve Optimizer: Shifts the CPU's voltage/frequency curve per core. Negative values = less voltage for the same speed (cooler, can boost higher if stable).
glossary.C-state: CPU sleep states used when cores are idle to save power.
glossary.CPPC: Lets Windows/Linux know which cores are fastest so it can schedule work on them first.
glossary.IOMMU: Hardware that isolates devices' memory access. Needed for PCIe passthrough to virtual machines; recommended on.
glossary.SVM: AMD-V hardware virtualization. Needed for Hyper-V, WSL2, VMware, VirtualBox, KVM, Docker Desktop.
glossary.SR-IOV: Lets one PCIe device (e.g. a NIC) appear as many devices to virtual machines.
glossary.Resize BAR: Lets the CPU access all of a graphics card's memory at once (Re-Size BAR / Smart Access Memory). Usually a free performance gain.
glossary.ReBAR: Lets the CPU access all of a graphics card's memory at once. Usually a free performance gain.
glossary.NUMA: Non-Uniform Memory Access: splits the CPU and memory into zones so programs can keep data close to the cores using it.
glossary.NPS: NUMA nodes Per Socket: how many memory zones the CPU is presented as (NPS1 = one big pool).
glossary.CSM: Compatibility Support Module: emulates an old-style (legacy) BIOS. Must be off for Secure Boot and Windows 11.
glossary.Secure Boot: Only lets signed, trusted operating-system loaders start. Required by Windows 11.
glossary.TPM: Trusted Platform Module: a security chip (or firmware) that stores encryption keys. Required by Windows 11 and BitLocker.
glossary.fTPM: Firmware TPM built into the AMD CPU.
glossary.PXE: Network boot: start the computer from a server on the network instead of a local disk.
glossary.BMC: Baseboard Management Controller: the board's separate management computer (ASMB11-iKVM) for remote control over the network.
glossary.IPMI: The standard protocol for talking to the BMC remotely.
glossary.SEL: System Event Log kept by the BMC (errors, power events).
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory: detects and fixes single-bit memory errors. Your RDIMMs support it.
glossary.RDIMM: Registered DIMM: server/workstation memory with a buffer chip; supports ECC and large capacities.
glossary.Q-Fan: ASUS automatic fan-speed control based on temperature.
glossary.ErP: EU low-power standby mode. Cuts nearly all standby power but disables wake features and USB power when off.
glossary.ASPM: PCIe power saving for idle links.
glossary.Bifurcation: Splitting one x16 slot into several smaller links (e.g. x4x4x4x4) so a riser card can hold multiple NVMe drives.
glossary.MT/s: Mega-transfers per second: the 'DDR5-5600' style memory speed number.
glossary.Tcl: CAS latency: clock cycles between asking for data and getting it. Lower = faster.
glossary.tRCD: Clock cycles to open a memory row before reading/writing it.
glossary.tRP: Clock cycles to close a memory row.
glossary.tRAS: Minimum clock cycles a row must stay open.
glossary.tRFC: How long a refresh takes. Very large; tightening it is an advanced tweak.
glossary.LN2: Liquid-nitrogen extreme overclocking. Leave LN2 options off for normal use.
glossary.Spread Spectrum: Wobbles clock speeds slightly to reduce radio interference. Off can help when overclocking.
glossary.Watchdog: A timer that resets or powers off the machine if software stops responding.

System Language.what: Language used for the BIOS screens.

Ai Overclock Tuner.what: The master switch for memory and clock overclocking. Auto runs the memory at its standard (JEDEC) speed - 4800 MT/s for your Kingston RDIMMs.
Ai Overclock Tuner.tip: To get the 5600 speed your DIMMs are rated for, choose EXPO and then pick Profile #0.

options.Auto: Standard, fully safe settings. Memory runs at 4800 MT/s.
options.Manual: Lets you set BCLK (base clock) and other clocks by hand. For experienced overclockers.
options.EXPO: Loads a speed/timing/voltage profile stored on your memory sticks (5600 or 5200 for your Kingston DIMMs).
options.DOCP: Loads an Intel XMP profile from the memory sticks. Not offered when the sticks also have EXPO.

EXPO.what: Which of the memory sticks' built-in EXPO profiles to load.
EXPO.tip: Profile #0 is the fastest (DDR5-5600 CL28 at 1.35 V). Profile #1 (DDR5-5200 CL36 at 1.25 V) is a gentler fallback if #0 isn't stable with all 8 DIMMs.

DOCP.what: Which of the memory sticks' built-in XMP profiles to load.

eCLK Mode.what: Whether the CPU's base clock is tied to the memory/PCIe base clock or set separately.

options.Asynchronous mode: BCLK2 drives the CPU cores separately from memory/PCIe (BCLK1).

BCLK1 Frequency.what: The base clock for memory and PCIe. Normally exactly 100 MHz.
BCLK1 Frequency.tip: Raising it overclocks memory and PCIe devices together and can corrupt data on drives. Leave at Auto unless you know why you're changing it.

BCLK2 Frequency.what: A separate base clock for the CPU cores only (asynchronous mode).

PCIE Frequency.what: Base clock for the PCIe slots. Normally 100 MHz.
PCIE Frequency.tip: Changing this is risky for graphics cards, NVMe drives and network cards. Leave at Auto.

Memory Frequency.what: Forces a specific memory speed instead of what Auto/EXPO picks.
Memory Frequency.tip: Leave on Auto and use Ai Overclock Tuner = EXPO to get your sticks' rated speed. Use this only to step the speed down (e.g. 5200) if you have stability problems.

FCLK Frequency.what: Speed of the Infinity Fabric - the internal link between the CPU's core chiplets and memory controller.
FCLK Frequency.tip: Auto picks a good value for your memory speed. Manual values that are too high cause instability.

CPU Core Ratio.what: Sets a fixed CPU multiplier (CPU speed = ratio x 100 MHz), turning off normal boosting.
CPU Core Ratio.tip: A fixed ratio stops the CPU from boosting individual cores above it and from slowing down when idle. For most workloads Auto + PBO is faster.

options.CPU Core Ratio: Type an all-core multiplier (e.g. 45 = 4.5 GHz on every core).
options.AI Optimized: ASUS picks an all-core speed from its analysis of your CPU and cooler.
options.Per CCX: Set a separate multiplier for each core chiplet (on the CPU Core Ratio (Per CCX) page).

CCX# Ratio (Rail#).what: CPU multiplier for one core chiplet (speed = ratio x 100 MHz). Only used when CPU Core Ratio is set to per-CCX.

Core VID #.what: Fixed voltage request for the cores on this voltage rail when using manual per-CCX ratios.

Dynamic OC Switcher.what: Switches automatically between your manual overclock (under heavy load) and normal boosting (light load), based on current and temperature thresholds.

Performance Bias.what: ASUS presets that tune internal CPU behaviour for particular benchmarks or workloads.
Performance Bias.tip: Auto/None is right for normal use.

CPU Core# Voltage.what: Voltage for one of the CPU core power rails.
CPU Core# Voltage.tip: Auto is strongly recommended. Too much voltage damages CPUs; too little causes crashes.

options.Manual Mode: Use exactly the voltage you type below.
options.Offset Mode: Keep the automatic voltage and add/subtract a fixed amount.

CPU Core# Voltage Override.what: The exact CPU core voltage to use (in volts) when the voltage is set to Manual.

CPU Core# Voltage Offset.what: How much voltage to add or subtract from the automatic value (choose + or - in the Offset Mode Sign line).

Offset Mode Sign.what: Whether the offset raises (+) or lowers (-) the voltage.

CPU VSOC Voltage.what: Voltage for the CPU's I/O die (memory controller, Infinity Fabric, PCIe).
CPU VSOC Voltage.tip: Auto. With 8 DIMMs at high speed this is sometimes raised slightly, but keep it under about 1.25 V.

VDDSOC Voltage Override.what: Exact SoC voltage when set to Manual.

VDD_#_S# / MC Voltage.what: Voltage for the CPU's memory controller.

VDDP Voltage.what: Voltage for the memory PHY - the CPU circuitry that talks to the DIMMs.

High DRAM Voltage Mode.what: Unlocks memory voltages above 1.435 V. Only for extreme memory overclocking.

DRAM VDD Voltage.what: Main voltage for the memory chips. Set automatically by EXPO (1.35 V for profile #0).
DRAM VDD Voltage.tip: Leave at Auto unless tuning memory by hand.

DRAM VDDQ Voltage.what: Voltage for the memory data bus. Normally equal to DRAM VDD.

Precision Boost Overdrive.what: Lets the CPU use more power and current so it boosts higher and stays boosted longer. The CPU still protects itself by temperature.
Precision Boost Overdrive.tip: Enabled/Enhancement levels give extra multi-core performance at the cost of more heat and power. Good cooling is needed on a 350 W Threadripper.

options.Disabled: Stick to AMD's stock power limits.
options.Enabled: Use the motherboard's higher power limits.
options.Enhancement: ASUS-tuned presets that raise limits in steps.

PBO Limits.what: Where the CPU's power and current limits come from.

options.Motherboard: Use the higher limits the board's power delivery can handle.

PPT Limit.what: Maximum total CPU socket power, in watts.

TDC Limit.what: Maximum sustained current from the CPU voltage regulators, in amps.

EDC Limit.what: Maximum short-burst current from the CPU voltage regulators, in amps.

VDD# TDC Limit.what: Sustained current limit for the second CPU core power rail, in amps.

VDD# EDC Limit.what: Burst current limit for the second CPU core power rail, in amps.

Precision Boost Overdrive Scalar.what: How hard PBO pushes voltage to reach higher boost. Higher = more voltage over time.
Precision Boost Overdrive Scalar.tip: Auto or 1X is kindest to the CPU long term.

CPU Boost Clock Override.what: Raises (or lowers) the CPU's maximum boost speed by up to 200 MHz above stock.
CPU Boost Clock Override.tip: Only helps if your chip and cooling allow it; combine with Curve Optimizer.

Max CPU Boost Clock Override(+).what: How many MHz to add to the CPU's maximum boost clock.

Max CPU Boost Clock Override(-).what: How many MHz to take off the CPU's maximum boost clock.

Platform Thermal Throttle Limit.what: The CPU temperature (°C) at which it starts slowing down. Lower = cooler and quieter, slightly slower.

Curve Optimizer.what: Undervolts (or overvolts) the CPU along its whole speed range. Negative counts lower voltage, which can let the CPU boost higher while running cooler.
Curve Optimizer.tip: Start with All Cores, Negative, 5-10 and test stability. Too much negative causes random crashes when idle or lightly loaded.

options.Per Core: A separate value for each of the 32 cores.

Per-Core Boost Clock Limit.what: Caps the boost speed of individual cores (in MHz). Mostly used to stop a weak core from being unstable.

Medium Load Boostit.what: ASUS tweak that lets the CPU boost harder during medium (not full) loads.

Peak Current Control.what: Limits brief current spikes. Auto is recommended.

Tcl.what: CAS latency - how many clock cycles memory takes to return data after a request. Lower is faster.
Tcl.tip: EXPO #0 sets 28 for your DIMMs. Values must be even.

Trcd Wr.what: Cycles to open a memory row before writing to it.

Trcd Rd.what: Cycles to open a memory row before reading from it.

Trp.what: Cycles needed to close a memory row before opening another.

Tras.what: Minimum cycles a memory row must stay open.

Trc.what: Minimum cycles between opening the same row twice (about Tras + Trp).

Twr.what: Cycles the memory needs after a write before the row can be closed.

Refresh Interval.what: How often memory is refreshed. Longer intervals are slightly faster but less safe when hot.

Trfc#.what: How long a memory refresh takes. Tightening it is an advanced tweak.

DRAM Timing Control.what: Hand-tuning of memory timings. Everything on Auto follows the selected EXPO/JEDEC profile.

CPU Rail# Load-line Calibration.what: Controls how much CPU voltage drops under heavy load. Higher levels keep voltage steadier (helps overclocks) but add heat.
CPU Rail# Load-line Calibration.tip: Auto is fine for stock and PBO.

CPU Rail# VRM Switching Frequency.what: How fast the CPU power stages switch. Higher = cleaner power, more VRM heat.

CPU Rail# Power Phase Control.what: How many power phases are active. Extreme = all phases always on (best for overclocking).

VRM Spread Spectrum.what: Varies the VRM switching speed slightly to reduce electrical noise. Disable when overclocking.

Clock Spread Spectrum.what: Slightly varies the base clock to reduce radio interference. Turning it off can help stability when overclocking.

SVM Mode.tip: Turn on if you use Hyper-V, WSL2, Docker Desktop, VMware, VirtualBox or KVM.

SVM Enable.what: AMD hardware virtualization (AMD-V) at the CPU level.
SVM Enable.tip: Keep enabled if you run virtual machines or WSL2.

Resize BAR Support.what: Lets the CPU access all of a graphics card's video memory at once (Re-Size BAR / Smart Access Memory).
Resize BAR Support.tip: Turn on for modern GPUs - it's a free speed-up in many games and GPU compute tasks. CSM must be off.

SR-IOV Support.what: Lets PCIe devices (like the X710 network ports) be split into many virtual devices for virtual machines.
SR-IOV Support.tip: Only matters for VM hosts; harmless to leave on.

Legacy USB Support.what: Makes USB keyboards, mice and drives work before the operating system loads (in the BIOS, boot menus, old OS installers).

options.Auto: Turn legacy support off if no USB devices are connected.
options.Disabled: USB devices only work inside UEFI-aware software and the OS.

USB Mass Storage Driver Support.what: Lets the BIOS read USB drives (needed to boot or flash the BIOS from a USB stick).

Network Stack.what: Loads the BIOS's network drivers so you can boot over the network (PXE/HTTP boot).
Network Stack.tip: Leave disabled unless you network-boot - it slows startup slightly.

options.RAID: Combine drives into AMD RAID arrays (needs AMD RAID drivers).

NVMe RAID mode.what: Lets NVMe SSDs on the CPU's lanes be combined into AMD RAID arrays.
NVMe RAID mode.tip: Leave off unless you're building a RAID - Windows needs the AMD RAID driver to see drives when it's on.

SATA Controller(s).what: Turns the SATA ports on or off.

SMART Self Test.what: Runs a quick drive health check (S.M.A.R.T.) at every start and warns if a drive is failing.

Restore AC Power Loss.what: What the PC does when power returns after a power cut.

options.Power On: Turn on automatically (useful for servers or remote machines).
options.Last State: Return to whatever it was doing before the power cut.

ErP Ready.what: EU ultra-low-power standby. Cuts power to almost everything when the PC is off.
ErP Ready.tip: When on, wake-on-LAN, USB charging and keyboard power-on stop working.

Power On By PCI-E.what: Lets a PCIe network card (including the onboard X710) wake the PC (Wake-on-LAN).

Power On By RTC.what: Turn the PC on automatically at a set date/time.

HD Audio Controller.what: Turns the onboard audio on or off.

Q-Code LED Function.what: What the two-digit Q-Code display on the board shows after startup.

options.POST Code Only: Show boot progress codes only, then go dark.
options.Auto: After boot, show the CPU temperature.

PCIEX16(G#)_# Bandwidth Bifurcation Conf.what: Splits this x16 slot into smaller links so a riser/adapter card can hold several NVMe SSDs.
PCIEX16(G#)_# Bandwidth Bifurcation Conf.tip: Use x4x4x4x4 for a 4-drive M.2 adapter card. Leave on Auto for graphics cards.

PCIE Speed Control.what: Whether you can force PCIe slot speeds (Gen 3/4/5) below.

PCIEX#(G#)_# Link Mode.what: Forces this slot to a specific PCIe generation. Lower it (e.g. Gen4) if a card or riser cable is unstable at Gen5.

M.#_# Link Mode.what: Forces this M.2 slot to a specific PCIe generation.

SMT Control.what: Turns the CPU's second thread per core on or off (64 threads vs 32 on a 9975WX).
SMT Control.tip: Leave on (Auto) for most work. Some games and licence-per-thread software prefer it off.

Core Performance Boost.what: AMD's automatic boosting above base speed. Turning it off locks the CPU near its 4.0 GHz base clock.
Core Performance Boost.tip: Keep on (Auto) for performance; disable only for testing or minimum power/noise.

Global C-state Control.what: Lets idle cores enter deep sleep states to save power.
Global C-state Control.tip: Leave on - it also helps boost because idle cores give their power budget to busy ones.

Power Supply Idle Control.what: How deeply the CPU idles. 'Typical current idle' can fix rare freezes with some power supplies when the PC is idle.

IOMMU.what: Hardware isolation of device memory access. Needed for PCIe/GPU passthrough to virtual machines and for Windows Kernel DMA Protection.
IOMMU.tip: Enabled is recommended on a workstation.

NUMA nodes.what: How the CPU's memory is presented to the operating system.

options.NPS1: One big memory pool - best for most workstation work.
options.NPS4: Four memory zones - can help NUMA-aware software (some databases, HPC).

NPS Mode.what: How many memory zones (NUMA nodes) the CPU is split into. NPS1 is best for most desktop/workstation use.

Memory interleaving.what: Spreads data across all memory channels for maximum bandwidth. Keep enabled.

DRAM ECC Enable.what: Error-correcting memory: detects and fixes single-bit memory errors. Your RDIMMs support it.
DRAM ECC Enable.tip: Keep on (Auto/Enabled) - it's one of the main benefits of a workstation.

Memory Context Restore.what: Skips full memory training on reboot by reusing saved results, so the PC starts much faster.
Memory Context Restore.tip: If you get memory errors after changing memory settings, turn it off once to force a full retrain.

TDP Control.what: Lets you set the CPU's thermal design power instead of using the default.

PPT Control.what: Lets you set the CPU's package power limit instead of using the default.

TjMax Control.what: Lets you lower the maximum temperature the CPU allows before throttling.

Determinism Control.what: Whether CPUs boost to the maximum their silicon allows (Performance) or behave identically from chip to chip (Power/deterministic).
Determinism Control.tip: Auto is fine for a workstation.

CPPC.what: Tells the OS how fast each core is so it can manage speed and power itself.

CPPC Preferred Cores.what: Tells the OS which cores are fastest so single-threaded work runs on them.

DF Cstates.what: Lets the Infinity Fabric sleep when idle. Disabling can slightly reduce latency at the cost of idle power.

AVX#.what: AVX-512 instructions. Used by some scientific, AI and video software; disabling only makes sense for testing.

SEV-SNP Support.what: AMD secure encrypted virtual machines. Only needed for confidential-computing VM hosts.

Gaming Mode.what: Turns off cores and SMT to mimic a smaller, low-latency CPU for older games.

Fast Boot.what: Skips some hardware checks so the PC starts faster.
Fast Boot.tip: Turn off temporarily if you can't get into the BIOS or a new device isn't detected.

Boot Logo Display.what: Shows the ASUS logo during startup instead of text messages.

POST Delay Time.what: Extra seconds to wait at startup, giving you more time to press Del or F8.

Bootup NumLock State.what: Whether Num Lock is on when the PC starts.

Wait For 'F#' If Error.what: On a startup error (e.g. no CPU fan detected), stop and wait for you to press F1.
Wait For 'F#' If Error.tip: Turn off if you use a pump/fanless setup that triggers a CPU-fan warning on every boot.

Option ROM Messages.what: Whether add-in cards (RAID, network) show their own startup screens.

Launch CSM.what: Enables the old-style legacy BIOS mode for very old operating systems or cards.
Launch CSM.tip: Keep disabled - Windows 11, Secure Boot and Resize BAR all need it off.

options.Windows UEFI mode: Enforce Secure Boot (needed for Windows 11 security features).
options.Other OS: Don't enforce Secure Boot (some Linux setups, unsigned drivers).

Secure Boot Mode.what: Standard uses the built-in Microsoft keys. Custom lets you manage your own keys (advanced).

AMI Native NVMe Driver Support.what: Use the BIOS's own NVMe driver so NVMe SSDs can be booted from.

Boot Option #%d.what: The order the PC tries boot devices in. #1 is tried first.

Chassis Intrusion Detection Support.what: Warns at startup if the case has been opened (needs a case switch connected to the header).

CPU Fan Q-Fan Control.what: How the CPU fan header controls speed.

options.Auto Detect: The board detects the fan type.
options.PWM Mode: Controls 4-pin fans with a speed signal.

CPU Fan Profile.what: Preset fan curve for the CPU fan.

options.Manual: Draw your own curve with the temperature/duty points below.

CPU Fan Q-Fan Source.what: Which temperature sensor drives the CPU fan's speed.

CPU Fan Step Up.what: How quickly the fan speeds up when temperature rises. Slower = less noticeable noise changes.

CPU Fan Step Down.what: How quickly the fan slows down when temperature drops.

CPU Fan Speed Low Limit.what: Below this speed the BIOS treats the fan as failed and warns you. Set to Ignore for pumps or zero-RPM setups.

Chassis Fan # Profile.what: Preset fan curve for this case-fan header.

Chassis Fan # Q-Fan Control.what: How this case-fan header controls speed (3-pin DC or 4-pin PWM).

BIOS Image Rollback Support.what: Allows flashing an older BIOS version than the one installed.

Publish HII Resources.what: Makes BIOS menu data available to the OS and BMC (for remote BIOS configuration via Redfish).

Flexkey.what: What the board's Flexkey button (normally Reset) does.

options.Safe Boot: Restarts in safe mode with default BIOS settings.

Load from Profile.what: Loads settings saved earlier in one of the 8 profile slots. Type the slot number (1-8). Press F10 afterwards to apply.

Save to Profile.what: Saves all current settings into a profile slot (1-8) so you can restore them later.

Profile Name.what: Label for the profile you're about to save.

OS Watchdog Timer.what: Resets or powers off the PC if the operating system doesn't finish starting within the timeout (the BMC watches it).
OS Watchdog Timer.tip: Only useful for unattended servers - needs management software in the OS to switch it off after boot.

OS Wtd Timer Timeout.what: Minutes to wait for the OS to start before the watchdog acts.

OS Wtd Timer Policy.what: What happens if the watchdog expires.

BMC DRAM SMBUS Switch.what: Whether the BMC or the BIOS reads the memory sensors (temperatures) over the shared SMBus.

SEL Components.what: Whether startup errors and events are recorded in the BMC's System Event Log.

Erase SEL.what: Clears the BMC event log at the next (or every) restart.

Configuration Address source.what: How the BMC's management network port gets its IP address.

options.Unspecified: Don't change what the BMC already has.
options.Static: Use the IP address you type below.
options.DynamicBmcDhcp: Get an address automatically from your router (DHCP).

Station IP address.what: The BMC's own IP address (for remote management via its web page).

Subnet mask.what: Usually 255.255.255.0 on home and small-office networks.

Router IP address.what: Your network's gateway (usually your router's address).
